findings.claim: The Mool Mantar qualities are listed as "timeless (akal)".
findings.truth: The Mool Mantar term is akal murat ("timeless form"). Akal on its own is not the phrase in the text, and the revision tip asks students to name the Sikh terms.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Mul Mantar: ikk oankaar, sat naam, karta purakh, nirbhau, nirvair, akal murat, ajuni, saibhang, gur prasad

findings.claim: "Mukti (also written moksha) is the Sikh term for liberation".
findings.truth: Moksha is the Sanskrit Hindu term, not an alternative spelling of mukti. The spec names mukti as the Sikh concept.
findings.evidence: spec Component 3 Option 5, The Afterlife: "The aim of mukti (liberation): GGS 11, 43"

findings.claim: "in Sikhism, the liberated soul does not dissolve into God without identity, but continues in a state of loving union and service to God", presented as a settled contrast with Hindu belief.
findings.truth: Sikh teaching on what survives at mukti is contested, and the common GCSE line is the opposite: the soul merges with God, pictured in the Guru Granth Sahib as light blending into Light or water into water (Sukhmani Sahib, GGS 278). Options: (a) replace with the standard merging image and drop the invented contrast with Hinduism; (b) keep the sentence but hedge it as one Sikh view; (c) delete the comparison and say only that mukti ends rebirth and unites the soul with God.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Sikhism (liberation section) does not support the claim; GGS 278 'as water blends with water, so does his light blend with the Light'

findings.claim: "Ik Onkar encapsulates the entire Sikh theological world view in two syllables."
findings.truth: Ik Onkar is three syllables (Ik-On-kar) and is written as a numeral plus a symbol, not two syllables. Rhetorical, will not cost a mark.

findings.claim: "The Guru Granth Sahib (page 349) affirms the value of seva and the community practice of sharing food together."
findings.truth: Ang 349 (Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak) teaches that God's light is in all and that class and caste count for nothing. It says nothing about sewa or shared meals. The spec cites GGS 349 for the equality of all human beings.
findings.evidence: srigranth.org ang 349, checked; spec Component 3 Option 5, The Oneness of Humanity: "equality of all human beings, including equality of men and women: GGS 349"

findings.claim: Key fact: "The Guru Granth Sahib (p.349) connects langar to sewa and equality."
findings.truth: Same mis-description of ang 349. The ang teaches equality; langar is the practice that expresses it.
A fabricated claim about examiner behaviour. House rule bans invented examiner or mark-scheme claims.

findings.claim: [2].marks: "Guru Granth Sahib (p.349) connects langar to selfless service."
findings.truth: Ang 349 teaches equality and that caste counts for nothing; langar puts that into practice.

findings.claim: [4].marks: "GGS p.349 affirms the value of community worship and service."
findings.truth: Ang 349 is about equality, not community worship. The accurate source point for this question is the Hukamnama read from the Guru Granth Sahib.

findings.claim: "The scripture describes all humanity as 'born from the same clay' (Guru Granth Sahib, pauri 349)".
findings.truth: That wording is not on ang 349. The clay and one-light imagery is Kabir's, on GGS 1349-1350 ("from the One Light the entire universe welled up"; "the clay is the same"). A page of the Guru Granth Sahib is an ang, not a pauri. Ang 349 does teach that God's light is in all and that there are no classes or castes.
findings.evidence: srigranth.org angs 349 and 1349, both checked; Wikipedia, Guru Granth Sahib (pages are angs)

findings.claim: [5].q: "Which page of the Guru Granth Sahib teaches that all people are 'born from the same clay'?" with answer "Guru Granth Sahib 349."
findings.truth: The flashcard drills a quotation-to-page pairing that is wrong. Ang 349 teaches that caste counts for nothing; the answer 349 is right for that teaching.

findings.claim: [2].marks: "(all from same clay / divine light in all)".
findings.truth: The mark scheme repeats the misattributed clay wording. Divine light in all is correct for ang 349.

findings.claim: [5].marks: "Guru Granth Sahib 349 explicitly condemns caste - 'born from same clay' - placing equality at the heart of revealed teaching."
findings.truth: A student who quotes this in a 15-mark answer is quoting a verse that is not at that ang. Ang 349 supports the point without the invented quotation.

findings.claim: "For 15-mark evaluations on authority, remember to include contrasting religious and non-religious perspectives."
findings.truth: This paper studies one world faith only. Contrasting views should come from within Sikhism (khalsa and sahajdhari, for example) plus a non-religious view. Writing about another religion wastes time. Not wrong enough to edit, but the wording invites it.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3 Component 3 (Route A): candidates are assessed on ONE option; diversity knowledge 'may be applied'

findings.claim: Unit-wide exam framing: 2, 5, 8 and 15-mark question types; no SPaG claim; no board named.
findings.truth: Checked and clean. The spec sets this paper at 1 hour, 25% of the qualification, 60 marks, compulsory questions, and puts SPaG in the other two papers only. No lesson claims SPaG on this paper, no lesson uses AQA or Edexcel tariffs, and no lesson names the board in prose or in a flashcard.
findings.evidence: spec lines 176-200, 2607, 4346-4360; grep of all three lessons for 'Eduqas' and 'WJEC' returned nothing

summary: The unit's Sikh doctrine, Guru names and dates, festivals, Five Ks and ceremony detail are sound, and the exam framing is correct for this paper. The real fault is a chain of wrong attributions to Guru Granth Sahib ang 349: lesson 3 invents a 'born from the same clay' quotation there (the clay and one-light imagery is Kabir's at GGS 1349-1350) and lesson 2 makes the same ang teach sewa and shared meals. Nine of eleven edits repair that chain plus a fabricated examiner claim; the mukti-and-identity claim in lesson 1 needs Tom's ruling.
